commits.message:
fix(markup): route every consumer through the one markup crossing (rich-markup-pcp) (#101)

* fix(markup): route every consumer through the one markup crossing (rich-markup-pcp)

`src/core/markup.ts` exported two functions that turn a markup string into a
`RichText`, and the four call sites in `src/` were split between them under the
same import alias:

    plugin-aware:  renderables/progress.ts, renderables/table.ts
    plain:         renderables/prompt.ts, core/console.ts  (`render as renderMarkup`)

The import line read identically at all four, so the difference was invisible at
every point of use. A tag registered on `globalMarkupRegistry` resolved in a
table cell and was silently eaten by `console.print` — the path almost every
consumer takes — printing the content unstyled with nothing reported.

Both plain sites now import `renderMarkup`. Measured, not assumed:
`console.print("say [shout]hello[/shout] now")` emits `say HELLO now\n`, and
`Prompt.ask` shows `pick ONE: `. `test/core/markup-grammar.golden.txt` passes
unchanged, which is PR #96's measurement — `renderMarkup` is a strict superset
that delegates on both early exits — confirmed end to end rather than re-derived.

`render` is now module-private: the ticket's open question, decided. Exporting
the inner layer is what made this bug representable, and unexported the drift is
a compile error rather than a rule to remember. Rendering *without* plugins stays
reachable as a value — `renderMarkup(s, { registry: new MarkupRegistry() })` —
instead of as a second function name. That also retires a second exported
`RenderOptions` that collided by name with the unrelated one in `core/protocol.ts`.

`examples/claude-sessions/.../_common.ts` carried the identical alias beneath a
JSDoc that already claimed `renderMarkup`; the two now agree. The plugin demo
gains the bare-string `console.print` path — the usage that was broken, and the
one every markup doc teaches.

`test/core/markup.test.ts` asserts the built-in dialect through the public
crossing with an explicit empty registry, so it no longer binds to an internal
function and cannot be perturbed by another suite's global registration.

* fix(markup): reject an overlapping plugin pair where it is detected

The top-level filter in `pairPluginTags` decided containment from where a pair
*opened* and nothing else. That one comparison read two different shapes as one:
a contained pair, which the recursion re-discovers when it renders the outer
pair's inner slice, and an overlapping pair, which has no contiguous region at
all. Both were skipped, so the overlapping pair's closing tag was orphaned into
the trailing slice and the built-in parser rejected it there — naming the wrong
tag, for the wrong reason.

Routing `console.print` through `renderMarkup` put that on the main path: with
two plugin tags registered, `[aa]x[bb]y[/aa]z[/bb]` printed `xyz` before (unknown
style names, non-strict nesting) and raised `MarkupError: Closing tag [/bb]
doesn't match any open tag` after.

Overlap stays rejected, because it is unrepresentable rather than unimplemented
— a handler receives `children` as one contiguous slice, so a region straddling
another pair's closing boundary has nothing to hand it. A style span may overlap
because it annotates; a plugin pair may not because it replaces. What changes is
that the rejection now happens where the shape is known and says so:

    Plugin tag [bb] overlaps [aa]: plugin tags must nest, because a handler
    receives one contiguous slice. Close [/bb] before [/aa].

Deliberately untouched: an inner plugin tag that never closes (`[aa]x[bb]y[/aa]`)
gets no entry in `pairs`, so it never reaches the overlap test and still renders.
The obvious alternative — rejecting whenever a closing tag's match is not the top
of the stack — would have broken it, which is why the test lives in the filter
rather than the walk. Pinned, along with sequential pairs and the built-in
dialect's non-strict nesting.

Found by review on PR #101.
